Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. (p.
1) On the beautiful Mount Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels, Caṇḍī, desirous of hearing [the truth], questioned Śaṅkara. 1-1.
Śrī Caṇḍikā said:
[I bow to Him who is] formless, devoid of qualities, free from praise and blame,
eternal, the creator of all, beyond description, and perfectly immovable.
Devoid of perception and the like, peaceful, what is its form and how is it established?
O Lord of Gods, from that [source], by what form does origination arise? (1–3)

Śrī Śaṅkara said: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme reality— the Vaiṣṇavī who transcends all letters, who is the abode of the qualities yet transcends the qualities, and who is devoid of both praise and blame.
O Goddess of the Gods, because she is devoid of form, eternal, free from passion and the like, and the one who brings about her own manifestation for the sake of worship; || 1-5 ||
O Śivā, listen to that form by which the universe is born:
from space (ākāśa) wind is born, and from wind the sun is produced.
From fire water is produced, and from water the earth is produced;
O Daughter of the Mountain, by means of these five elements the cosmic eggs come into being. (1.7)
Indeed, for the sake of uplifting the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), O Anantaka, it rests upon the back of the Tortoise;
and upon his head, many cosmic eggs remain like grains of sand.
Within the midst of the waters of compassion, the Tortoise moves eternally;
I alone, moreover, protect [the world] again and again with my trident.
Śrī Caṇḍikā said:
O Maheśvara, knower of reality, tell me what is the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and what is the manner of creation within it; indeed, what is its shape?
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
O Pārvatī, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) indeed takes the form of living beings and possesses various bodies;
for that which is called the body of the cosmic egg includes everything from the gross to the minute.
In the center of that is Meru, and likewise the goddesses along with the Sasa and Kulācala mountains;
indeed, the mountain named Sumeru extends from the base to the summit.
O Maheśānī, Bhūrloka and the other worlds, as well as the seven heavens, are situated respectively below the navel and above the tips of the fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, the seven netherworlds reside upon a finger;
[therein is She] who is formless in Satyaloka and whose nature is that of the Great Light.
Her self concealed by illusion, she has the form and appearance of a campaka flower;
she is devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs, yet she possesses the nature of the moon, the sun, and fire.
When she, having cast off the bond of Māyā, becomes divided into two and turns toward [the Supreme], the conceptualization of creation arises through the differentiation of Śiva and Śakti. (1.16)
"O Pārvatī, in the first [birth] a son named Brahmā is indeed born.
Śrī Kālikā said: 'Listen, my son, O most formidable one; perform your marriage with diligence.'"
Having heard this, Brahmā then spoke respectfully, "O beloved, there is no mother other than you; O beautiful one, grant me power."
Having heard that, the Mother of the Worlds gave from her own body Mohinī;
she was the second Great Vidyā, Sāvitrī, the supreme Kalā.
Having obtained union with her, perform the expansion of the Vedas;
become the effortless creator of the universe upon the circle of the earth.
In the second [period], a son is born who is Viṣṇu, the locus of the quality of sattva.
Listen, my son: perform your marriage with great care, for it is most formidable. (1.21)
"By the mere sight of you, a man becomes free from desire;
I speak the truth, O Mother Śivā, grant me [this] among those who enchant. (1.22)
Having extracted the power from her own body, Kālikā gave that great vidyā,
Vaiṣṇavī Śrīvidyā, to him, O Supreme Lord.
Relying upon her, Mahāviṣṇu protects the entire universe;
in the third [birth], the son born is Mahāyogī Sadāśiva.
Seeing him, that Mahākālī became filled with contentment and joy;
"Listen, O son, great yogi, and take my words to heart. (1-25)
Without you, what man is there? Without you, what enchanting woman is there? Therefore, O Śiva, O Supreme Bliss, grant me marriage.
"O Mother, it was said that there is no enchantress (Mohinī) apart from you;
this is true, O Mother of the World, for there is likewise no man apart from me. (1.27)
"And while this body still remains, I will not perform the marriage;
O Mother, if you have compassion, take on another body. (1-28)
At that moment, Mahākālī gave Bhuvaṇasundarī;
as Kālī was the primordial being, so too was Bhuvaṇasundarī.
Relying upon that, the great yogi withdraws the entire universe;
Śambhu is eightfold in division, and Śakti likewise becomes eightfold.
O Supreme Goddess, by this [means] the great vidyās beginning with Kālikā are indeed [attained];
thus, O Beloved, the description of Brahman has been told to you. (1.31)
"It must be guarded with effort, O beloved, so that the arising of knowledge may occur.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Nirvāṇatantra*, in the dialogue between Caṇḍikā and Śaṅkara. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter. Śrī Caṇḍikā said:
"O Mahādeva, by your grace, I have heard the exposition of Brahman."
Now I wish to hear how the creation upon the earth came to be.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how creation comes into being.
In Satyaloka, Mahākālī was embraced by Mahārudra.
Expansive in form like the *caṃpaka* flower, having the appearance of the moon, sun, and fire, they are joined with the beginningless Puruṣa; those known as *jīvas* are portions of Him. (2-3)
O Goddess, just as sparks flash forth from a blazing fire,
so too the supreme mercury (vidrum) that has fallen from it, even when it reaches the ground— || 2-4 ||
At that very moment, O Daughter of the Mountain, the Goddess suddenly becomes united with union even among stationary objects, insects, beasts, and birds.
O Supreme Goddess, he obtains eighty-four lakhs of births;
thereafter, O Mistress, he attains that human body which is so difficult to find.
Since he possesses a human body and is the master of both merit and demerit, for that reason he obtains birth again and shall undergo death once more. (2.7)
O Daughter of the Mountain, it is certain that one is born and dies indeed due to the bond of karma within the eighty-four hundred thousand various wombs.
Śrī Caṇḍikā said: O Lord, how does one obtain birth, and how does death occur?
O Mahādeva, I wish to hear the manner of that in accordance with reality.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:

Whatever action is performed here, its fruit is experienced in the next world; like a caterpillar moving from one blade of grass to another, the individual soul (jīva) passes from one body to another. (2.10)
"Having attained a subsequent body, he abandons his former body.
Having heard this, Caṇḍī questioned the Supreme Lord.
"But when the subsequent body has been cast off, how can there be the offering of funeral cakes and so forth?
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain: that very body is indeed a body of māyā. (2-12)
O Supreme Goddess, this illusory body is of the nature of air and not otherwise;
for this body, being of the nature of air, resides in space without any support. (2-13)
And therefore, by the offering of the *piṇḍa*, the vital air (*vāyu*) becomes more stable;
first, O Goddess, the head is produced, up to the limit of the wheel (*cakra*). (2.14)
Then, having gone to the city of Yama, they experience that which is due to their dharma and so forth;
and after that, others experience something further, provided that no other karma remains.
Then, by Yama’s command, the individual soul departed for the means of attaining Brahman;
therefore, according to one's karma, if that [human] body should be difficult to obtain again— (2.16)
By the power of fortune, one obtains the Great Vidyā from the supreme Guru;
O Maheśānī, if by the power of fortune one should attain the knowledge of reality. (2-17)
At that very moment, as long as the creation of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) lasts,
she grants supreme liberation to the Brāhmaṇa and great liberation to the Kṣatriya.
By the grace of Mahāvidyā, she attained silver and rebirth in the same world as the Śūdra born from her thigh; indeed, there shall be no returning again. (2-19)
When all liberation occurs within Śiva at the end of the vast cosmic egg, then the final extinction (nirvāṇa) of everything certainly takes place; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Caṇḍikā said: O Supreme Lord, what indeed exists outside the vast Brahmāṇḍa?
I wish to hear all of that, if you have affection for me. (2.21)
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Outside the region of this universe, many other universes exist;
how could I possibly describe the measure of that which is infinite?
She alone is all that is emanated; she alone is everything, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Nirvāṇatantra*, in the dialogue between Śrī Caṇḍikā and Śaṅkara.
Chapter Three.
The illustrious Śiva said:
By nature men are born; by nature the world is created.
O Goddess, just as a bubble arises from water and dissolves back into the water, so it is. (3-1)
Everything is born from primordial nature (prakṛti) and dissolves back into it;
therefore, through union with primordial nature it is born, and never otherwise. (3-2)
The Goddess is certainly born from Prakṛti as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
likewise, at the time of dissolution, she is again absorbed into Prakṛti. (3.3)
All twice-born men are indeed Śāktas, neither Śaivas nor Vaiṣṇavas, because they worship the Goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable. (3–4)
Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the Gāyatrī, who is honored by the four Vedas,
renowned as the Mother of the Vedas, and the bestower of the fruits of the three aims of life.
Having extracted Hālāhala, one should extract the navel-syllable;
joined with the left ear, one should again extract it with the waters.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, [the mantra] consists of the letter *ka* joined with *rṇa*, followed by the letter *ra* on the head (*mūrdhni*),
then the letter of Varuṇa (*va*) joined together, and after that, the seed-syllable of the Moon (*caṃdra-bīja*).
One should extract a single *vyāhṛti* joined with the sound 'na' and the letter 'kha';
then, having extracted that word, [one should place] that of Savitṛ immediately after it.
Having uttered "vareṇyam," one should say "bhargodevasya dhīmahi" and "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt," followed immediately by the Praṇava.
Then, O Maheśānī, by reciting "The Gāyatrī has been studied, and immediately after that, the Praṇava," one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
And in the middle portion of the *dhiyaḥ* [mantra], there are two *yakāra*s;
in each of those places, O Great Goddess, is the infinite scripture itself.
Having recited this, O Maheśānī, one becomes joined [with the goal] at that very moment; one should read the letter *ya* in place of the letters *aṃ* and *ya*. (3-12)
And he is known as a Cāṇḍāla because of the sin of Brahman-slaughter [committed] day after day;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, it has been revealed out of affection for you. (3.13)
The Śāvitrī is the supreme knowledge, difficult to obtain even within the three worlds;
by the mere grasping of it, one becomes worthy of worship by the earth—of this there is no doubt. (3-14)
O beloved, listen to the mantra for the ritual placement upon the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) which I shall speak:
one should place two *praṇavas* in the lotus of the heart and the syllable *bhūḥ* in the region of the head.
The wise one should place *bhūr* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*),
*bhuvaḥ* on the armor (*kavaca*), *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* on the three eyes, and *svaḥ* on the pair of hands.
One should sequentially assign *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
Listen, O beautiful lady, to the visualization (*dhyāna*) by means of which a person should perform worship after having meditated upon it. (3.17)
She is described as being white in color, likewise dressed in silk garments,
and adorned with white unguents, flowers, and ornaments.
The Goddess resides within the solar orb or has gone to the world of Brahmā;
she holds a rosary and is seated upon a lotus throne.

Oṃ! You are splendor; you are semen; you are immortality; you are the name of the abodes. You are the beloved of the gods—the Gāyatrī who is one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, and four-footed. 3-20.
Salutations to You, the Fourth State, the manifest reality, the giver, and that which transcends the realm of dust (the material world).
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable.
Having meditated again, O fair-faced one, he should offer a flower upon these three seats;
first, having placed a triangle, he should place a hexagon outside of it.
A circle, an eight-petalled lotus, and outside that a square provided with four gates— this is declared to be the Sāvitrī-yanttra.
Having performed the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa) and other rites, one should worship her, the bestower of the three aims of life;
O Supreme Goddess, [one should recite] the entire mantra beginning with "hātyaha" and so forth.
Having recited [the name], he should say "pādyaṃ" (water for the feet), followed by the Sāvitrī joined with it;
thereafter, the mantra consisting of renunciation, according to the extent of his means.

One should worship with many vehicles; otherwise, O beautiful woman, it is prescribed for Brahmā that one may worship with substances consisting of water, such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, in the absence of [other] materials.
Having worshipped her, one should sacrifice to the Goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable;
by that, the [sins] produced in ten births and those committed in the past are destroyed. (3.27)
A thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī destroy even a great sin;
she was born from the mouth of Maheśa and resides in the heart of Viṣṇu. (3-28)
"Permitted by Brahmā, O Goddess, go as you desire"—having uttered this mantra, the wise one [should place it] in the left hand of the Goddess. (3.29)
One should then offer the fruit of the recitation; thereafter, one should recite hymns and so forth.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is declared to consist of one hundred thousand recitations performed according to the prescribed rule. (3.30)
Thereafter, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Following the oblation, one should perform a libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of one-tenth of the oblation. (3-31)
Thereafter, one should perform a sprinkling (abhisreka) that is one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa);
following that, one should provide a meal for Brahmins that is one-tenth of the sprinkling.
Then the Goddess becomes perfected, bestowing the fruits of the three aims of life;
and the majesty of this mantra has been proclaimed by the four Vedas.
Now listen attentively to the method for the mantra of purification:
[one should perform it] on the ground, on the head, and in the sky; in the sky, on the ground, and on the head.
On the head, on the ground, and likewise in space and in the Yajurveda, O Mistress of the Gods;
and [the one] with the Atharvaveda, O Goddess—now hear [of him] in the Ṛgveda, O Daughter of the Mountain. (3.35)
One should practice the acquisition of the bow upon the head, on the ground, in the void, likewise upon the head, on the empty ground, and likewise upon the crown of the head. (3.36)

Regarding the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā": those mantras consisting of eight-syllable feet, when used for ritual sprinkling (mārjana) in their proper sequence, bring about the destruction of all sins. (3.37)
And because of this transgression, Cārvaṅgī incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step;
therefore, out of affection for you, I have revealed this entire sequence. (3.38)
Having purified the hymn of praise and the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the wise one should bow down.
The Goddess said:
"O God, that which is the fourth state (*turiya*) is indeed the effulgence, the Supreme Self. (3-39)
"If Śiva is situated outside in the lotus, how can there be an act of salutation?
Śrī Śiva said:
Mahādeva, likewise the supreme guru, resides within the lotus of the head."
O Goddess of the gods, there is indeed nothing equal to that which is worthy of worship in the three worlds;
the mantra-practitioner should contemplate that form as the fourfold external Guru. (3–41)
Those who are born from his portions as well as other teachers and people,
and likewise all the Brahmins, are established as partial incarnations (aṃśāvatāra).
Whenever one should meditate upon these externally and directly before the eyes,
at that time one should abandon such mental reflection within the great thousand-petaled lotus.
O Goddess, when the vision is direct and external, the best of practitioners, contemplating that Brahman, should perform prostrations and other rites. (3-44)
Upon merely seeing these [beings], one should perform prostrations and other such acts;
if one fails to do so out of delusion, one will become a vessel for calamity. (3-45)
Having observed a Brahmin and others, as well as a student and the three types of ascetics, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before them by a mere glance, O Girijā. (3.46)
Even one joined with a great sin (mahāpātaka) becomes liberated at that very moment;
yet if, through delusion, he does not perform [the rite], he shall become possessed of a great sin. (3-47)
Having observed his red garment as well as his bodily ornaments,
and having seen him with a staff in hand and a trident, [the devotee] performs three circumambulations.
The best of practitioners should perform [this]; otherwise, he would become a sinner.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Nirvāṇatantra. 3.
The Fourth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, what is that *nyāsa* like, and what is the state of the *avadhūta* like?"
Or what kind of person is a celibate student (brahmacārī), and what kind is a householder? 4-1.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess of the gods, one should meditate upon the form of Vīra as possessing a body of divine luster, holding a staff,
and always adorned with ashes and other ornaments.
The form of the householder Kaulika is that of a celibate student (brahmacārin),
while the divine form of the householder is adorned with sandalwood paste and other ornaments.
He is the father-form of all, the householder who embodies the virtuous man.
Śrī Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the Great Brahmāṇḍa. (4-4) p. 6)
O Dear One, in the center of Mount Meru is the abode of all the gods;
there, in the middle region, the river Mahāvīrā is eternally situated.
O fair-faced one, Śatyaloka is situated at the upper region of Sumeru,
while Rasātala, O Maheśānī, resides in its lower part.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, there are fourteen worlds in sequence within Meru;
above the seven netherworlds (pātālas) is the Brahma-lotus.
That four-petalled lotus is indeed downward-facing in the center of the earth;
within the seed-vessel at the center of that lotus is the beautiful circle of earth.
The seven oceans are situated in the form of a circle;
in the center is Jambudvīpa, which is four-cornered and beautiful.
The triangle is the abode of Madana; Kandarpa is the presiding deity. O Śivā, the form of the Aindra-bīja is indeed "Laṃ," and its vehicle is the lordly elephant.
In the triangle, the abode of Madana, Maheśvara exists in the form of the Bindu;
O Maheśānī, Māyā-śakti has the form of a coiled serpent.
The Liṅga is encircled by that very [coil] in the form of three-and-a-half rings;
it remains forever covering the aperture of the Liṅga with its mouth directed toward the sky.
O lady of excellent hips, the seed-syllable of Indra is located on the left side of the linga;
it is the perfectly accomplished abode of Brahmā, most beautiful above the nāda.
In that very place dwells Brahmā, the creator of the universe and lord of progeny;
and on his left side is Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas and queen of the gods.
Having obtained her grace, you always expand the creation;
the abode of Brahmā, which is of the nature of reality, extends for a hundred thousand yojanas.
All that, O Supreme Goddess, is contained within the day called the Ṛgveda;
it is a triangle, O Supreme Goddess, consisting of sixty-two squares.
That indeed is declared to be the mountain, for it is the refuge of all the gods;
O fair-faced one, it is outside that triangle, first to the west and then to the east.
O Goddess, look at the stationary mountain, the insect, the most excellent animal, the bird, and humans and so forth; what is there on the surface of the earth that does not exist [within you]? 4-18.
Outside the triangle, O Girijā, are the mountain Vahurūpaka,
Nīlācala, Mandara, and the mountain Candraśekhara.
The Himalaya, Sumeru, Malaya, and Bhasmaparvata—O Goddess, you dwell in these four corners; this is the group of seven principal mountains.
O Goddess, from the peak of these mountains arose a mountain of many forms,
containing various abodes of the gods as well as the abode of the Dānavas.
Right there, O Pārvatī, grasses, shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants of various forms were born as the most sinful beings through the power of their past actions.
They are born and they die by the very path previously described.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Yoga," in the Nirvāṇatantra. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter. Śrī Śiva said:
Above this lotus is an auspicious lotus named Bhīma.
Likewise, there is a circle with six petals, adorned with four gates.
In the center of the lotus, within the seed-vessel, is the enchanting Bhuvarloka,
which is always resplendent with a red color like vermilion.
Fashioned by the Discus-wielder with a cloth dyed red with vermilion, Viṣṇu shall dwell above it, with Śrī and Vāṇī at his left and right. (5.3)
The world is created by Brahmā and protected by the wielder of the discus;
that creation is indeed named Vaikuṇṭha, for it is the abode of various gods.
To the right side of Vaikuṇṭha is Goloka, which enchants all;
there resides the goddess Rādhikā, two-armed and holding a flute.
This place, served by hosts of sages such as Nārada who have mastered the Vedas, is like Vaikuṇṭha; there is no other location equal to it in knowledge and tranquility.
Just as one sees everything here in the middle and likewise on the outside,
so too do all those dwelling on the earth perceive the celestial sphere.
All the deities, beginning with Indra, endowed with various enjoyments and adorned with various jewels, stand there for the sake of the red [flower]. (5.8)
If one perceives the world as consisting of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), resplendent with arms, clad in yellow garments, possessing a radiant form, and adorned with a forest garland; || 5-9 ||
In this way, all the devotees were made to shine in Vaikuṇṭha;
they bore the name Viṣṇu, sang the praises of Viṣṇu, were followers of Viṣṇu, and possessed the form of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess, that form which is the sphere of Goloka does not exist in Vaikuṇṭha without the song of Viṣṇu;
nor does that form exist in the mortal world. (5.11)
Or rather, what exists within visual knowledge or through the yoga of meditation?
It is the Goddess, pure and consisting of the sixfold nature, adorned by various deities.
Right there Kailāsa shines; right there is the city of Brahmā;
right there is the city of Vaikuṇṭha, and right there is the abode of the Sun.
O beloved, the abode of the Moon is indeed right there, as is the abode of Kandarpa;
and there is the abode of all the gods, adorned by celestial maidens and others.
In the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) is the Yogamaṇḍira of Śrī Viṣṇu known as Golaka;
it is the gross, wondrous, and enchanting form of Śrī Viṣṇu, whose nature is Sattva.
What greatness of that place can I possibly describe now, where the two-armed upholder of the earth shines eternally? (5.16)
The great Viṣṇu is formless, yet even in every moment he possesses form;
whenever he assumes a form, at that very moment he is the holder of the flute.
Then Viṣṇu, who consists of pure being, will certainly protect him;
O Supreme Lord, right there he shall attain the great liberation of a Vaiṣṇava.
Thus, the greatness of this place has been declared by me in brief;
I am not able to describe it in detail even in hundreds of future births.
Outside the seed-vessel (bījakośa), however, is encircled the circle of water;
the water is beautiful in its proportions, like the ocean of milk (kṣīroda).
Above the Dhustūra [region], there is a circle of water, brilliant white in its circular form, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons and appearing like a mass of light. (5.21)
O beautiful one, all the rivers such as the Gaṅgā shine forth right there,
and all the deities beginning with Indra appear there incessantly.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and those named [others], as well as kuṣmāṇḍas and bhairavas,
always indeed manifest in embodied form through the chanting of the Vedas.
In Mālava, she is always measured by Navarāga, O beloved;
in Malāra and Atharva, she is likewise always so, but not so again in Vasantā.
The Creator should always perform the recitation of the Yajurveda with the *hiṇḍola* melody;
likewise, O Śivā, one should recite the Ṛgveda in Karṇāṭa and Śrīrāga.
This [portion] has been specified as the recitation; beyond this, it is unspecified.
Therein itself reside sixteen thousand passions. (5.26)
In that very place, sixteen thousand rhythmic measures (tāla) shine forth; through the singing of the flute by Murāri, all these rhythmic measures are produced. (5-27)
The sages and people always sing with that rhythm and that melody created by the Creator;
indeed, they divide the various parts of that melody. || 5.28 ||
Spring and the other seasons abide there perpetually;
[he beholds] the flute-player adorned with various minerals and flowers.
In that very place, the goddess Rādhikā, indulging in various delights of pleasure,
was saying, "O Beloved, play the flute-song that utterly fascinates!"
With whatever sound the constant arising of desire is produced, with that very passion and that rhythm, perform the song with diligent effort. (5-31)
Thus endowed with bliss, the great goddess of splendor and grace,
Rādhikā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, always shines upon the left side.
Making this sole petition with devotion, Śrī Rādhikā said:
"Whether they be mortals endowed with devotion to You, or those possessed of [divine] devotion... (5.33)
[I meditate upon] Mahāviṣṇu residing in Goloka, two-armed and holding a flute,
the Lord ever endowed with bliss, shining in my company.
"O you who are dear to me, tell me specifically what the means are for those mortals who meditate in this manner."
The Blessed Lord said:

"O lady of beautiful limbs, listen; I shall grant the state of ultimate attainment to those who worship Me by whatever means and in whatever manner they do, for I am always affectionate toward My devotees. (5.36)
Furthermore, for those humans who chant "Ādhaurādha" and "Kṛṣṇa," I shall grant them a good state here; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, those people who worship me through the path of non-existence (abhāva-mārga) and through the path of mantra—they are always equal to me. (5.38)
That woman who always worships me as inseparable from Puruṣa is heard to be equal to you at all times; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether they speak of the Couple with devotion or even without devotion, through your devotion I shall grant them the supreme goal; listen, O Rādhikā! (5.40)
My devotees never go to the abode of Yama;
this is the truth, the truth, again the truth, the truth, the truth indeed, O Rādhikā.
Having heard this, the goddess Rādhikā, who is affectionate in love,
lay upon the lap of Mahāviṣṇu, tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
"O Goddess, listen with diligence to this world of Viṣṇu and its extent.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Nirvāṇatantra. 5.
The Sixth Chapter. Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Above this lotus is the Great Lotus, which is very difficult to attain.
By which the form of a blue-colored lotus with ten petals and filled with water [is perceived]. (6.1)
That lotus, blazing with those [petals] along with the moon, is exceedingly beautiful;
within its central seed-vessel (bījakośa), the perfectly perfected seed-syllable of fire (vahnibīja) dwells eternally.
O Goddess, outside that, in one-third of the area, is the Svastika resembling nine suns;
this is called Svarloka, worshipped by all the gods.
The seed-syllable of fire (RA), always mounted upon a ram,
together with the letter LA, is indeed located right there as the seat of great delusion.
The great vidyā Bhadrakālī is beautifully adorned on the left side;
the great vidyā Bhadrakālī is eternally the performer of destruction. (6-5)
The world is created by Brahmā and protected by him in the form of Viṣṇu;
as the Supreme Goddess in the form of Rudra, she is eternally the cause of its destruction.
He should withdraw [the universe] in the form of Rudra together with Bhadrakālī;
O Goddess Caṇḍikā, what is there that cannot be accomplished through the contemplation of Rudra?
That form which was previously described as the all-enchanting sphere (golaka),
in its universal manifestation within the world of Rudra, is indeed fourfold.
The world of Rudra is a great heaven, four times superior even to Goloka;
it is eternally bestowing great liberation, and Rudra is its bodily ornament.
Bhadrakālī is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) who bestows the state of Rudra;
whatever is ordained by Viṣṇu, she is joined with it in the form of Kālī. (6.10)
Therefore, O dear one, Kālī the Great Goddess and Muralīdhara are always to be worshipped with effort; by doing so, one shall become the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha.
O Goddess, the lord of Goloka, who is devoted to praise and devotion,
becomes a guardian of the worlds through the grace of Kālikā.
For the sake of protecting the worlds, Muralīdhara, accompanied by his consort,
shall worship Bhadrakālī and dwell eternally in Goloka.
Viṣṇu always honors the grace of Kālikā;
moreover, Viṣṇu, who is devoted to great courage, is the protector of the goat.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the glorious Nirvāṇatantra. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter. Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Above this lotus is a pure lotus, beautiful to behold.
It is adorned with twelve petals, red in color, resembling the bandhūka flower.
In the center, within the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa), is an auspicious six-cornered mandala with a lotus that bestows fruits exceeding one's desires and is as pure as vermilion.
In the center of the mandala is the beautiful seed-syllable of Vāyu;
it is the living seed-syllable of Vāyu, resplendent with four arms.
O Bhuvaneśānī, that Vidyā which is the sovereign of the three worlds, the Lord worshipped by all, and honored throughout the three realms; (7-4)
That Goddess resides on the left side of Īśvara;
O auspicious one, O Sovereign of the Gods, this Maharloka is the place of worship.
Right here, the best among those who know yoga perform mental yoga;
it is made of crystal, O lady with beautiful limbs reddened by vermilion.
Therefore, all human beings perceive the celestial light;
the gods, endowed with all their limbs, abide there eternally.
Those dwelling on earth behold that fiery splendor in the form of a wheel;
all those destined for the heavenly world remain in heaven, O Pārvatī.
Brahmā shall dwell in the Bhūrloka; Janārdana in the Bhuvarloka;
and Śambhu, the eternal agent of dissolution, shall dwell in the Svarloka.
He is the Lord of Brahmā and the others, the creator of all, the Sovereign (Īśvara),
the master of all things, the essential nature itself, the maker of all, and the Lord of the gods.
And the Supreme Lord is the creator of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth;
O Goddess, Goloka has been described as that which is eternally adorned with His form.
Therefore, O Goddess Śivā, Maharloka is a hundred times more beautiful than that [Janaloka], and it is a hundred times more extensive; indeed, everything there is a hundredfold greater.
O Supreme Goddess, how can I describe the greatness of Maharloka? It is a hundred times greater than Goloka in every respect. (7.13)
He who dwells in Maharloka, intent upon the common nature of the two,
[attains] from that very state one hundredth part of Goloka, which possesses the flute-player.
Having received his command, he is suddenly created by the Lotus-born Brahmā;
by that same command, he becomes the two-armed holder of the flute who protects the worlds.
For in this way, in the form of Rudra, he withdraws the entire universe;
since he is the creator of all, O Goddess, he is therefore the Supreme Lord.
Īśvara is the creator of all, devoid of qualities, immovable, and auspicious;
yet without the Goddess Bhuvaneśī, he is not even able to stir. (7.17)
The Lord was almost always like a cripple; indeed, it was not possible for him to walk.
Yet, by propitiating Bhuvaneśī, that Lord became the master of all.
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, she is the bestower of liberation through austerity alone;
she is the Mother of the Universe and the goddess who effects the protection of the universe. (7.19)
The giver of liberation to all worlds, the bestower of release, the Mother of the Universe—without Bhuvaneśī, the Lord is unable to accomplish anything. (7.20)
For this very reason, that Goddess is the bestower of liberation and possesses all forms.
Thus, I have related to you a brief description of Maharloka.
In brief, O Mistress of Others; now listen with reverence to another [instruction].
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Nirvāṇatantra. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter. Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Above this is a stainless lotus, the cause of the enchantment of all.
Endowed with sixteen petals, it is the destroyer of the darkness of delusion.
Just as fire exists within smoke, so too, O beloved, is the Janaloka, which consists of light,
situated within the beautiful pericarp of the lotus.
Outside of that is a lunar disc for the pacification of those blinded by great delusion,
adorned by hosts of gods, singers, and sages.
This place here is a hundred thousand times superior to Goloka, yet it is extremely difficult to attain;
furthermore, it possesses divinity, captivates the mind, and is likewise vast.
O Goddess, [the merit] is a hundred thousand times that of Goloka; of this there is no doubt.
In the seed-vessel (bījakośa) on Maṇidvīpa is the supreme six-cornered yantra.
In the center of the yantra is a bull whose body is half that of a great lion;
upon it is Gaurī forever, and on her right side is Sadāśiva.
He has three eyes and five faces, with three eyes on each face;
his limbs are adorned with ashes, he is silver-colored, and he has a protruding belly.
The God wears a tiger skin, is adorned with a garland of jewels,
is the bestower of desired objects upon the worlds, and the destroyer of the fear of the worlds.
He is the producer of liberation for the worlds, the bestower of knowledge upon the worlds,
the giver of the state of Brahman to his worshiper, and he is worshipped by Viṣṇu.
The all-pervading Lord, who brings joy to all, is the sovereign Ardhanārīśvara;
in some places the Lord consists of light, and in others he is devoid of form.
He is the worshipful form of the gods and the sovereign form of the gods;
he is the eternal bestower of liberation to his devotee, that Lord Viṣṇu who grants all boons.
By means of bilva leaves, she bestows her own union upon the worshiper;
she is Śivā, who, having made the Lord of Goloka her devotee, protects him. (8.12)
O Caṇḍikā, what is the use of elaborating upon the majesty of that god?
She is Gaurī, the mother of the world, who bears half of Śambhu’s body. (8-13)
She is Mahāgaurī, composed of the three qualities (guṇas), while the wielder of the Pināka bow possesses but one quality;
having attained union with her, Sadāśiva becomes the creator of all.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Nirvāṇa Tantra. || 8 ||
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Above this lotus is the lotus of knowledge, which is very difficult to attain.
It is joined with two petals, like the orb of the full moon.
One should remember the city of Cintāmaṇi within the seed-vessel in the center of the lotus;
in its midst is a nine-cornered yantra, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Indeed, in the center of that is the seed-syllable of Śambhu, possessing form in the shape of a swan;
the swan is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, while the one with form is the embodiment of Śiva. (9.3)
And the *tāra* (om), along with *kurvarāroddhā*, possesses the wings of going and coming;
it is the pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, adorned with three *bindus*.
And the abode of this Swan is in the sky filled with lotuses;
thus, on the lap of that Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa) is Paraśiva.
On her left side is Siddhakālī, whose nature is eternal bliss;
having obtained her grace, Maheśvara is the creator of all.
O auspicious one, this world of austerity (tapoloka) is very difficult for all the gods to attain;
it is there that the gods, beginning with Brahmā, practice meditation and yoga.
O Śivā, even through mental effort, nor by yoga, nor by austerity,
can the world of Tapas belonging to Golaka be attained, for it is four hundred thousand times greater [than others].
Those gods who dwell in the worlds of Brahmā, those such as the Suras in Vaikuṇṭha,
and those who reside in the world of Śambhu— they all remain devoted to him with supreme devotion.
O Auspicious One, because you were not arrogant even through asceticism, you have attained the world of asceticism (tapoloka).
O Goddess, let your two eyes be equal to that world of asceticism among all the worlds.
For she is indeed the worlds: Maharloka; she is Rūpya in Janaloka;
she is Yujya in the Tapalokas; and Nirvāṇa is twice above that.
Therefore, the gods beginning with Brahmā always desire the world of Tapas;
its greatness cannot be described by me.
Thus, O beloved, I have described to you the characteristics of the six heavens;
by knowing which, both I and the practitioner become liberated while living.
By the knowledge of which one never again enters a mother’s womb;
one attains long life, health, and sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (9.14)
And all the Purāṇas, O Pārvatī, have been spoken by me alone;
yet within that form of mine, no manifest form exists.
And within that [song], there is hidden knowledge; therefore, nothing at all is understood.
For it is thus, O fair-eyed one, that in the Vedic scriptures, [the truth lies] within the song.
Since there is no knowledge of the Word (Śabdajñāna), nothing at all is understood, even by that man who knows the eighteen Purāṇas along with the Vedāṅgas. (9.17)
One should always practice listening to his ancient texts;
one should never listen to a reciter who merely moves his lips [mechanically] but lacks knowledge of the text. (9.18)
For this is the defining characteristic of the scripture, while other explanations appear differently;
and the very nature of the Śabdabrahman has issued forth from my mouth. (9.19)
No doubt whatsoever should be entertained if [the practice] bestows liberation;
through doubt, one goes to the Raurava hell along with one's ancestors. (9.20)
Having made his knowledge stainless and his intellect stainless thereafter, he becomes endowed with great devotion and devoted to the welfare of all living beings. (9.21)
If, having realized that [the self] consists of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), one listens to this Tantra, then one attains liberation; this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. (9.22)
Whatever fruit is obtained from hearing the eighteen Purāṇas, and whatever fruit is obtained from hearing the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs— [that fruit is attained here]. (9.23)
And gold equal to Mount Meru for the Guru who is the embodiment of Brahman;
O Supreme Goddess, [one may also offer] the earth with its seven continents and its abundant crops.
If one should give [this] with a spirit of devotion, O Supreme Goddess, O Śivā, to one who has mastered the Vedas, from that indeed comes manifold fruit. (9.25)
O lovely-limbed one, if anyone hears even a single chapter of this tantra, they will certainly obtain a fruit ten million times greater than that. (9.26)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Nirvāṇa Tantra. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter. Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Above the lotus of knowledge is a true lotus with six petals.
A great lotus with its face turned downwards is situated upon the summit of Sumeru.
O Maheśānī, his leaf is endowed with all powers;
it is white, red, yellow, black, and even green.
Variegated with variegated forms, adorned with many colors;
in one moment white, in another moment red, and in another moment beautiful yellow. (10.3)
At what moment, O beloved of beautiful limbs, does it assume a white color, at what moment a supreme green color, and at what moment a variegated form?
Thus, O Goddess, that lotus is always adorned with various kinds of colors.
Just as one who has entered the light [of the sun], so indeed is the ball. || 10-5 ||
O Goddess, the lord of Golaka, who is devoted solely to the state of devotion,
and the lord of Kailāsa, should always practice the yoga of meditation.
Thus Brahmā and the other gods, Indra and the other lords of the thirty-three, all remained constantly established in divine states, devoted to praise and devotion. (10.7)
O Maheśānī, there itself are one hundred thousand forms of Muralīdhara;
O beloved, there are one million forms of Śiva and one hundred thousand forms of Brahmā.
O Supreme Goddess, every day the worlds of the cosmic egg come into being;
in their midst, Brahmā should establish the Lord of Kamalā.
One should perform the installation of Śiva, who possesses manifold forms, in that very place;
for thus, O Supreme Goddess, one should duly install the various powers (śaktis). 10.10.
Within every universe, however, one should perform the installation of the universe after having fashioned the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā, endowed with their various powers.
Within the Brahma-lotus on the earth dwell humans and other beings; O Goddess, all these are cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), and within them are the worlds.
Therein are the seven netherworlds (pātāla), and right there also are the seven heavens;
thus, in this sequence, all fourteen worlds reside within the entire body.
O Supreme Goddess, there is no doubt that a Brahmāṇḍa exists within every body;
thus has been described the characteristic of both the external region and the Brahmāṇḍa. (10.14)
That which exists in the very center, wherein the fourteen worlds reside— that indeed is the body of the Goddess, situated in the midst of the great cosmic egg (mahābrahmāṇḍa).
Thus, O Goddess, within this Brahmāṇḍa, there are many such varieties;
all those great Brahmāṇḍas are likewise born of Śarāri.
(13) Even upon the earth, those very fires take on the form of water;
within the great Brahmāṇḍa, indeed, a vast Brahmāṇḍa resides. || 10-17 ||
Within that, O Goddess, are living beings, and within that are the worlds;
there is a distinction according to the path of emanation, characterized by the divisions of gross, subtle, and so forth.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever kind of thing exists within the great Brahmāṇḍa,
all that indeed, O Queen of the Gods, is contained within the center of the vast Brahmāṇḍa.
Therefore, within the body in the form [of the subtle body], there are the fourteen worlds;
in the manner of creation, there is certainly no distinction from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 10-20 ||
For Sthūla, Kṣudra, Cāru-aṅgī, Medaka, and Paricāraka—
within the seed-vessel in the center of the lotus are the fourteen worlds.
The abode of every deity is manifold in form and serves as their support;
in the midst of that is Satyaloka, the causal ground of Mahārudra.
Fashioned from gold of ten-fold brilliance by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu),
the circle of the waters of the quarters was like the orb of the full moon.
On all sides were *pārijāta* trees, and in the center was the *kalpa*-tree;
near the *kalpa*-tree stood an excellent celestial palace.
Resembling the rising sun, adorned with four gates,
provided with a gentle breeze, and embellished with perfumes and incense.
In the center of that, O Goddess, is a pedestal with a jeweled lion-throne, O Beloved;
there resides Mahākālī, the supreme worshipper, in the form of the letter KĀ.
Having veiled his own self through Māyā, he remains therein with equanimity;
he alone is Mahārudra, and he indeed is Mahāviṣṇu. (10.27)
O Mahābrahmā, that very Self is distinguished only by name;
it is a single form, though threefold by name as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. || 10-28 ||
For one whose mind dwells on diversity, liberation is not found;
therein, O fair-eyed one, millions upon millions of cosmic eggs are born. (10.29)
Therein he should duly place Brahmā, therein Hari, and therein Rudra;
thus having fashioned the creation of the cosmic egg, the eternal Viṣṇu [remains].
Just as he creates the individual soul and the physical form of a living being,
so too does the attributeless one eternally create the manifold universe of Brahmāṇḍa.
Though devoid of qualities and in the form of a physical body, he is indeed the cause of spiritual perfection;
some say he is Brahmā, while others proclaim him to be Viṣṇu.
Some say that in the Great Primordial (Mahāpūrva), Rudra is the one stainless God;
the God, joined with the primordial Śakti, has a form shaped like the letter *ca*.
The letter *ī* is like a lamp within a net, having the form of the moon, sun, and fire;
it is the great light, formless, and like a perfectly incinerated sphere of air. (10.34)
In the world of truth, within the seed-vessel, in the auspicious abode of the wish-fulfilling gem,
one should meditate upon the stainless God seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
In his presence, she should worship her own beloved husband as the God who is intent on worship and meditation, with a belly shining like silver.
One should meditate upon the Lord, endowed with a beautiful mouth and a lovely face, whose very nature is radiant, as being united with his beloved and established within one's own form. (10.37)
Just as they behold a mountain within the depths of a mirror, so should one contemplate the God within the thousand-petaled great lotus. 10.38
For this, O beloved, is indeed the abode of the Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode of liberation;
it is the direct abode of the Nirguṇa and the abode of Mahākālī, O Śivā. (10.39)
In that very place abides the eternal, the immutable, and the immovable, whose form is supreme bliss—the Lord of the worlds, both transcendent and immanent. (10.40)
The Goddess Kālī is eternal bliss supreme, the illuminator of time;
she is the primordial power Mahākālī, O Lord, who brings about liberation. (10.41)
And just as trees are born upon the earth and dissolve back into the earth, so too does that which was born as a bubble in water dissolve back into the water. || 10.42 ||
Just as a water-born creature produced in a river dissolves back into the dense cloud from which it arose,
so too do the gods, beginning with Brahmā, emerge from Kālikā.
Likewise, at the time of dissolution, O Goddess, it dissolves again into that [source];
without the knowledge of Śakti, liberation leads only to mockery. (10.44)
O fair-eyed one, Brahmā exists as one part, Janārdana as another part, and Śambhu exists as yet another part of Kālikā. (10.45)
That other [state] is like the great ocean to the mahālīna and the rest; just as water in a cow’s footprint is [insignificant], so are the deities beginning with Brahmā. || 10-46 ||
O Śivā, what could a cow’s hoofprint know of the water of the ocean?
Therefore, neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu knows it, O Śaṅkara; how much less so [anyone else]? (10.47)
When Kālī brings about creation, the gods and others are born from her;
likewise, at the time of dissolution, they are again absorbed into her.
Therefore, Kālī bestows nirvāṇa, while Puruṣa is the giver of heaven;
furthermore, he is situated in the southern direction of the Sun.
Frightened, they flee in every direction from her named Kālī;
therefore, she is celebrated throughout the three worlds by the name Dakṣiṇā.
The male principle is said to be the right [side], while the female power (śakti) is declared to be the left;
having conquered the right with the left foot, she bestows great liberation.
Therefore, she is celebrated by the name Dakṣiṇā throughout the three worlds,
because through Kālī, the attributeless Puruṣa is brought forth and withdrawn.
Therefore, she who is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of Viṣṇu, Kālikā, the Mother of the World, is celebrated by the name Dakṣiṇā throughout the three worlds. (10.53)
That Kālī possesses a form with specific features, yet she takes the form of a chickpea;
she is devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs, and she is the embodiment of the moon, the sun, and fire.
O fair-faced one, her abode is said to be Satyaloka;
that place, O sinless one, is always to be prayed for by all the gods. (10.55)
O fair-eyed one, what greatness of that place can I possibly describe now, when it is but a single petal of a thousand-petaled lotus? (10.56)
The abode consisting of a thousand globes cannot be described even in a thousand lifetimes or with a hundred million tongues.
Indeed, I am not able to describe the beauty of that single petal;
therefore, O Pārvatī, O lady of excellent limbs, you must cease [your questioning]. || 10-58 ||
What can I say of the splendor within the filaments?
In their midst is the goddess Karṇikā, and in her midst is the seed-vessel (bījakoṣaka).
In the center of the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa), however, is the supreme ocean of nectar,
a circle of auspicious water extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
In the center of that, O Śivā, is Maṇidvīpa, extending for a thousand yojanas;
all around it are Pārijāta trees and an excellent grove of Kadamba trees.
In its center was a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), and there stood an excellent celestial palace (jyotirmaṇḍira),
provided with four gates and adorned with golden ramparts.
Accompanied by a gentle breeze and endowed with fragrant flowers,
thousands of celestial maidens are devoted to his service.
In the center of that is the Goddess, whose nature consists of fifty syllables;
above her, O Maheśānī, O Śivā, is a jeweled lion-throne.
Mahākālī and Mahārudra have the form of the letter Na;
they are the eternal great light, appearing like a lamp within the net of Indra (indrajāla). || 10-65 ||
Thus, O beloved, I have described to you the seven heavens in their proper order;
having heard this, conceal it with care and never reveal its form to anyone.
Out of great affection, O Goddess of gods, this has been revealed in your presence;
it has been spoken by me in brief, for it cannot be told in detail.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Satyaloka," in the *Nirvāṇatantra*, within the dialogue between the illustrious Caṇḍikā and Śaṅkara.
The eleventh chapter. Śrī Caṇḍikā said:
"O Mahādeva, by your grace I am pure, and not otherwise."
Now I wish to hear the knowledge of reality, which is very difficult to attain.
Śrī Śaṅkara said: My mind hesitates regarding the exposition of knowledge concerning reality;
O Pārvatī, I am weary of hearing such discourses on worldly existence.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain by what clarity of knowledge Viṣṇu, who rests upon the quality of sattva, [is so; and likewise] Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds. (11.3)
Through the grace of the knowledge of reality, Śambhu is the agent of dissolution;
and all others who are liberated, they too [attain it] through the grace of reality. (11.4)
O Supreme Goddess, how can the knowledge of reality be described by me?
O Mistress of the Gods, desist; do not ask again and again.
Having heard these words of his, the daughter of Śaṅkara spoke this speech:
"If you do not tell me the truth, O Mahādeva, O Lord. (11.6)
"I shall give up my life before him; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the truth that is most difficult to attain."
O beautiful one, having heard this with effort, O cowherd, [abandon] liquor, meat, fish, oysters, and sexual intercourse, as if they were your own kin.
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, these five principles lead to the cause of liberation and nirvāṇa; through the drinking of wine, one attains the eight sovereign powers and supreme release.
By the mere eating of meat, one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person;
by the mere eating of fish, Kālī becomes manifest. (11.10)
Merely by practicing with a mudrā, one becomes worthy of worship by kings, assuming the form of Viṣṇu;
through sexual union, the great yogi becomes equal to me—of this there is no doubt. (11.11)
But in another tantra, O Goddess, it was previously told by me;
and the majesty of this dharma was already explained by me long ago.
O beloved, this knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation and nirvāṇa;
it is that very place where the five principles (pañcatattva) meet together as one. (11–13)
I go to that very place; those men are always equal to me.
That woman is the form of Kālikā; when she dies, she is absorbed into her.
Those men who possess virtuous forms and are devoted to the knowledge of reality are declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta); they are of the nature of Brahman and not otherwise. (11–15)
Even she, though joined [to others], is destined for great liberation among the Kṣatriyas and the rest,
O supreme mistress of the Brāhmaṇas, if she is devoted to the ultimate reality.
Truth, truth, and again truth:
it dissolves into the Supreme Reality, just as water dissolves into the midst of water, O Supreme Goddess. (11.17)
In that very way, through service to reality, one merges into the Supreme Self.
Thus, O beloved, I have told you the knowledge of reality which bestows liberation. 11-18.
Through that clarity of knowledge, the accomplishment of liberation occurs without doubt;
for just as without the earth there is never any cause for stability.
Just as there can be no cause for the destruction of thirst without water,
O beloved, so too there can be no destroyer of darkness without the sun.
Just as nothing is cooked without fire through the application of effort,
O Goddess of Gods, so too the rain of nectar does not arise without the moon.
O Beloved, just as birth cannot occur without a mother’s womb, O Goddess, so too liberation does not arise without the knowledge of reality. (11.22)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, protect this with great effort;
thus, those endowed with divine disposition shall always possess the knowledge of reality.
O sinless one, that reality should always be practiced by those endowed with the state of heroes;
one should not do so in the abode of a beast, nor within the sphere of perception of a beast.
Nor [should one perform it] in the presence of an animal, nor within the range of an animal's vision; otherwise, upon seeing a bird or an insect, one should certainly not perform it. (11.25)
O wise one, listen to the method for attaining perfection, by performing which one shall achieve success;
having brought forth the single Śakti, the practitioner should always remain as one alone. (11.26)
The Kaulika should worship with great effort by means of the five principles;
having done so, he shall attain perfection, which is not within the range of vision of anyone else.
The worship of the Śrīcakra should be performed only where it is truly secluded; for the sake of attaining wealth, success will never arise there if others are present nearby.
In that very place one's desires are fulfilled where one worships the Cakra;
through the worship of the Śrīcakra, longevity, health, and sovereignty shall arise. (11.29)
There is no doubt that there will be an increase in fame, an increase in glory, and a share in liberation;
the fulfillment of desires, the perfection of knowledge, and the grace of the Goddess shall arise. (11.30)
He who performs the worship of the Śrīcakra is indeed the imperishable Lord himself;
he is as if he has performed thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of recitations.

Whatever fruit one obtains by performing sacrifices, that same fruit is obtained through the worship of the Kaulika; likewise, whatever fruit one might obtain by giving gifts such as ponds, wells, and tanks.
If one should worship the Cakra, the fruit thereof is multiplied ten millionfold;
that food becomes equal to Mount Meru, and a single drop [of water] is like the ocean. (11.33)
O Goddess, if one should worship the wheel with a flower as large as Mount Meru, and if a man afflicted by disease should abide in its center, [he shall be freed]. (11.34)

Indeed, one should worship with the understanding that it is Śiva, and one should avoid delusion in that regard; for those who perceive what is merely a reflection of the sun [as the sun itself], [they are mistaken]. (11.35)
Just as the sun appears in the waters of the Gaṅgā and likewise in shallow water, yet there is no blemish upon the sun—the sun alone remains constant. (11.36)
In the same way, O Supreme Goddess, there is no fault in the practitioner;
by the mere worship of me, he becomes one with my self and absorbed in that. (11.37)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, there is no defect in semen;
semen is supremely pure, the power that is the cause of liberation. (11.38)
Furthermore, that woman who possesses power devoid of worship and devoid of recitation, yet holds [the mantra] in her hand, is Kālikā herself. (11.39)
No delusion should be entertained here if she grants liberation;
for that woman who has come to the circle of the wheel is possessed of delusion. (11.40)
For seven births, that woman shall be a Cāṇḍālī, devoid of a husband;
this is the fate for any woman who treats such a woman with contempt.
"He is a Caṇḍāla devoid of wealth and sons, and it is not otherwise.
Thus, O beloved, I have told you the knowledge of reality that bestows liberation. (11.42)
O Great Goddess, those in whose bodies the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) has been imparted by me shall never again enter a mother’s womb.
Those men are declared to be liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and they are of the very nature of Śiva.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall now describe the characteristics of a Kaulika.
That deity in whose mantra-sādhana a particular conduct has been prescribed, one who is distinguished by that conduct is indeed proclaimed as a Kaulika. (11.45)
This knowledge of reality has been declared for the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, Cāndra, and Sulocana [sects]; now listen with diligence to that which pertains to the Vaiṣṇava.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Knowledge of Reality," in the Nirvāṇatantra.
Chapter Twelve.
The venerable Caṇḍikā said:
Listen, O Lord, supreme bliss, sovereign of my life-breaths!
O Lord of the world, tell me that which is the true reality of a Vaiṣṇava. (12.1)
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen to the truth concerning the Vaiṣṇava, O fair-hipped Trilocanā;
[listen to] the truth of the Guru, the truth of the mantra, and the truth of the letters, O Queen of the Gods.
O fair-faced Pārvatī, there are the reality of the deity, the reality of meditation, and the five realities; among these, I shall first explain the reality of the venerable Guru out of affection.
The wick combined with oil, which is the splendor of Brahman residing within the body, becomes ignited by the preceptor through the imparting of the mantra. || 12-4 ||
For the body of a deity is certainly produced from the individual soul (jīva);
therefore, its self is undoubtedly of a divine form. (12-5)
But that which is the seed of the Lord is itself of the nature of the Imperishable;
by that [seed], the body of a living being consists of phonemes—of this there is no doubt. (12.6)
O Supreme Goddess, the phonemes of the mantra merge into their corresponding letters;
O Goddess, this is the reality of the letters which constitutes the essence of everything that exists for me. (12.7)
I am not myself the god, nor is there another; I am the stainless one whose form is that of the deity.
I meditate upon the divinity everywhere, even in grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like.
Through meditation one obtains everything; through meditation one becomes the very form of Viṣṇu.
Through meditation one attains perfection; without meditation, there is no perfection.
Thus, O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, I have told you about the Vaiṣṇava;
through this knowledge, one attains immortality and becomes the very form of Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Goddess, the mortal who should practice this knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) proclaimed by me shall partake of heaven and be glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Those mortals who always contemplate liberation with their minds never go to the abode of Yama.
Thus, O Goddess of the gods, I have told you the truth concerning the Vaiṣṇava;
by the knowledge of which one attains immortality—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narration of Viṣṇu’s Suffering," in the Śrī Nirvāṇa Tantra.
The thirteenth chapter: Śrī Caṇḍikā said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme ten-syllabled mantra, by the mere hearing of which even a fool becomes the very form of Viṣṇu. (13-1)
O Goddess of the gods, if one recites a Śakti-mantra without knowing that great mantra, even if it is a Pu-mantra, he shall become a Brahma-rākṣasa. (13-2)
Even if one were to possess knowledge there without having first understood that great mantra, it is the consensus of the God that such a person would nevertheless go to hell. (13-3)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme ten-syllable mantra:
the seed-syllable of Māyā, Lakṣmī, Kālī, and the noose. (13-4)
"O Dear One, 'gagana' (sky) is the seed-syllable of the bird, and from that comes 'pavahnikāntā' (the beloved of fire).
Thus, O Caṇḍī, this unsurpassed ten-syllable mantra has been declared to you. (13.5)
By knowing this, one attains immortality; of this there is no doubt.
Merely by grasping it, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (13.6)
O Caṇḍī, by the mere grace of this [mantra], one shall attain nirvāṇa.
O Supreme Goddess, one should recite these ten syllables over a staff.
From this [mantra], the great mantra is born; there is no doubt in this matter.
All deities, possessing that very form, are certainly born from the ten syllables. 13-8.
And the practitioner of the Mahāvidyā sees the ten-syllable fire;
in this world he is poor, and in the next he becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa. (13.9)
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, the Guru should cause the ten-syllable mantra to be heard with effort;
the best of practitioners should merely listen to it and recite it.
O Goddess, he who causes one to hear the Hāshārṇa and Sa-na-ye is the supreme guru; indeed, such a true guru is remembered as being equal to the giver of the mantra itself.
O Goddess, he who gives the Daśārṇa [land] is indeed the supreme guru;
just as the river Nāsukalāpagā is to the Marataraṅginī.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, there is no mantra equal to that of Daśārṇa;
and if there were a woman equal to you, there would likewise be a man equal to me.
There is no one equal to Daśārṇa; for I declare that his mind is like pure gold of ten-fold luster. (13–14)
O beloved, at that time he should recite the ten-syllable mantra;
O Supreme Goddess, this ten-syllable mantra is superior even to the Śrī-prāsāda mantra. (13–15)
"In the great tantra of the Ūrdhvāmnāya, I shall proclaim the majesty;
hereafter, I will describe that form which is the wielding of the staff. (13–16)
He was a virtuous householder and a Brahmin who discoursed on the Veda;
having renounced all worldly means, he was ever devoted to righteousness.
Having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, he maintained equanimity toward all castes;
he was equal toward son and enemy, and equal toward gold and a clod of earth.
And a disposition of compassion should exist toward everyone—toward a son, a friend, and an enemy;
likewise in gain or loss, in victory or defeat, in censure as well as in prosperity. (13–19)
In this body, there is no connection [to liberation] regarding death at the end of the age; for one who lacks knowledge of Brahman, no understanding exists through mere reflection. (13-20)
O worshiper of the gods, this dharma of renunciation belongs to him alone and not to anyone else;
the observance of *saṃnyāsa* must be performed by a Brahmin for the sake of liberation. (13-21)
Whatever brahmin carries the staff, he himself becomes Nārāyaṇa;
by the mere act of carrying the staff, they are born four-armed. (13-22)
Endowed with all the proper characteristics, a Brahmin should go forth;
and having gone there, upon seeing one who carries a staff, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
You alone, O God, are the Lord of Gods; you alone are the one who provides protection.
You alone are the one to be praised by the worlds; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Having heard this, the wielder of the staff respectfully asked the man:
"Who are you? To whom do you belong? Tell me, indeed, by what means did you come here? (13-25).
Having heard those words, the brahmin spoke, making himself known.
For, though born from the state of being a Brahmin, I am unliberated yet possessed of discernment.
I have no parents present before me, nor do I have a wife, sons, or others; my mother and father have passed away, as have my brothers and children. (13-27)
Afterwards, upon the destruction of my beloved, I shall indeed become utterly destitute;
therefore, O Lord, grant me a supreme refuge. (13.28)
"O best of the twice-born, make true what was spoken in my presence.
By the fault of speaking falsely, you shall be deprived of the path of Brahman. (13.29)
"It certainly exists; there is no doubt. O Supreme Goddess, speak before me of that beloved woman who stands in the prime of her youth. (13.30)
Indeed, everything is fruitless for him who would inflict punishment;
O Goddess, he who inflicts punishment while his parents are still living [commits a grave offense]. (13.31)
O Supreme Goddess, for one who still possesses attachment to a wife and likewise to a son, the undertaking of renunciation is indeed in vain.
"Both the guru and the disciple bestow that which is called Raurava.
Having heard such firm words as these, Āḍa, his senses conquered, [acted accordingly]. (13.33)
The guru should grant him the gift of renunciation and eternal liberation;
first, the guru should cause him to hear the ten-syllable mantra. (13.34)
Then, having heard this, one should cause the journey to Mahāvartman to be undertaken;
thereafter, one should proceed with speed for a *krośa* or two *krośas*.
When questioned by the Guru, he replied with three kinds of prostrations:
"Stay, stay, O mighty-armed one! Do not depart, leaving me behind. (13.36)
"O Paramahaṃsa, there is no disciple on this earth equal to you;
you must forgive my offense, for you are Viṣṇu himself, assuming a physical form. (13.37)
You alone are the one to be praised by the worlds; you alone are worshipped by all;
you alone are the supreme Haṃsa; stay, stay indeed—do not depart!
"O Goddess, because he spoke these words to Daṇḍin along with his disciples, that supreme Haṃsa has been utterly deluded on your path. (13.39)
For the very purpose of seeing him, those deities,
accompanied by women and Kimpuruṣas, arrived from the intermediate spaces and from all directions and sub-directions.
At this time, O observer of excellent vows, the staff-bearer should pacify the supreme disciple by uttering many "phut" sounds while reciting this mantra: (13.41)
By means of hissing breaths and the application of air, he should again employ the vital breath;
indeed, for him, rebirth occurs at that very moment.
Having envisioned the next birth, the Guru should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāra).
Having brought [the disciple] near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should perform the rite of first feeding solid food (annaprāśana). (13.43)
Having addressed [the deity] by such-and-such a name, one should cast a flower into the fire;
having thus established [the deity] by name, one should perform the great installation.
Then, O Goddess, the *piṇḍa* was given for the sake of the disciple’s lack of knowledge.
Listen, O disciple of great fortitude; my word is the heart of the Guru. (13.45)
In that interval, however, he alone possesses authority over the earth;
this body is of the nature of a corpse, there is no doubt. (13.46)
One who has desisted from mantras everywhere should be known by their diet and dress; [this is] your meal, O Brāhmaṇa. || 13-47 ||
The five principles (pañcatattva) should always be practiced by one who has conquered the senses and attained the state of realization;
one should always perform mental worship and [always maintain] the [inner] state.
Always strive diligently to renounce mental attachment to enjoyments.
Having conquered the six internal groups, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa himself; of this there is no doubt, even if he merely wields the rod of punishment. (13.50)
In the paternal lineage, [there are] seventeen mothers... [and] for the beloved one, the seventh indeed shall be Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (13.51)
Having heard these words of his, [the disciple] said:
"The five principles (pañcatattva) are always to be practiced; tell me, from what source is the benefit? For where there is punishment, there are many disciples..."
Alternatively, one should practice the mental discipline in the midst of heroes.
Indeed, one should go into the presence of a householder who possesses knowledge of reality;
one must travel even a very great distance to where the leader of the lineage resides.
But having seen the teacher's wife, he should offer alms with a concentrated mind. || 13-56 ||
"O Mother, give me alms; I, the one with earrings, shall satisfy [the ancestors].
Having spoken thus, the bearer of the staff should then perform the great ritual arrangement (mahāsaṃsthāra).
Having brought [the materials] to the edge of the sacrificial pit, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule;
then, holding the hand, one who possesses the sacrificial fire should offer eight oblations of clarified butter.
One should perform the specific marking with the staff in reverse order;
thereafter, one should diligently apply the inner sacrificial thread.
One should place the mantra, together with the disciple, at the end of the crest (śikhā) in the middle of the vessel;
then, by means of the root mantra, one should place the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) upon that very same [vessel]. || 13-60 ||
Having smeared the betel nut with ghee-clay, one should then purify it;
thereafter, one should place the betel nut within the middle of the staff while reciting the root mantras.
Then the wise one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and bring that betel nut;
O Dear One, he should purify that pair of sacrificial threads at the crest-lock (śikhā).
There, one should mutter the root mantra one thousand times,
O beautiful lady, and then cause the mantra of Kālikā to be heard.
Alternatively, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the mantra of Tārā, which is extremely difficult to obtain;
having carefully recited the root mantra together with betel nut and ashes.
By consuming it, at that very moment he visibly becomes one who bears a staff and wears the sacred thread;
of this there is no doubt—he becomes a man who is Nārāyaṇa himself. (13.65)
Having brought a bilva leaf, one should bring one from a bamboo stalk;
on a bilva staff, one should diligently recite the mantra of Kālikā. (13.66)
Then, having performed the jīvan-yāsa (the placement of the vital breath), one should contemplate the staff as the Goddess;
one should then join the consciousness residing in the bilva fruit to the bamboo staff.
O Supreme Goddess, this staff is the very form of the chosen deity;
one should perform the placement of the staff in the right hand of the disciple. (13.68)
Having brought a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) belonging to Varuṇa, one should pour the water of Varuṇa into it;
then one should mutter the root mantra. || 13-69 ||
One should carefully cause him to put on a garment of red ochre and a loincloth.
Merely by wielding the staff, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa;
one should visualize Mahākālī above the staff as the wisdom of the Guru.
For you are indeed Nārāyaṇa in person, O you who are devoted to the dharma of compassion.
Neither mother nor father stands at the end of the punishment for a twice-born householder who enters another's home like a thief. (13.73)
The wise man should always recite the Nārāyaṇa [Hymn]; having heard this, even a householder should become supremely devoted with palms joined in reverence. (13.74)
And having seen the staff-bearer at the gate, one should prostrate;
O Goddess of Gods, taking the alms-food, one should proceed like a thief.
Thus, indeed, one should observe a three-night residence.
Having gone from there to the sacred ground (tīrthabhūmi), one should dwell there for seven nights;
then, upon seeing a staff-bearing Brahmin, one should prostrate according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess of gods, whether it be a vessel full of water or an empty water-pot,
by the mere sight of it, that vessel will certainly become full of water.
If he should not give [the gift] out of delusion, he would become a refuge for calamities;
for thirty thousand years, he would exist as a tree-shrub in the forest.
Thus, O Caṇḍī, the supreme practice of renunciation has been told to you;
it must never be spoken to heretics, even at the cost of one's life.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Nirvāṇatantra, in the dialogue between Caṇḍikā and Śaṅkara. || 13 ||
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how one becomes an Avadhūta.
One should know the hero to be one who is always devoted to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), born from his very form.
The beloved of the heroes should perform all ritual actions in that supreme form of renunciation which was previously described. (14.2)
O Goddess, one who possesses a staff should perform the necessary tonsure;
O Goddess, one should not perform the tonsure for anyone in whatever manner [arbitrary]. (14.3)
She has unadorned hair, a shaven head, and a prominent pair of breasts;
she is adorned with a garland of bones or likewise wears rudrākṣa beads. || 14-4 ||
In the Vīra [tradition], he should either be naked or wear only a loincloth;
with his body adorned with divine red sandalwood paste, he should make ashes his bodily ornament.
O Daughter of the Mountain, forgiveness, charity, austerity, and meditation do not exist in the state of a hero.
I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava; I am liberated, the leader of the Kula. (14.6)
Thus, the practitioner of mantra, intent on the true nature of reality, should always be endowed with the causal factors;
he should constantly practice the cultivation of pure consciousness and always attend to the primary cause.
(22) That man would become Śambhu himself in person, without a doubt;
through the state of a hero (vīrabhāva), the Brāhmaṇa attains the liberation of Nirvāṇa. || 14-8 ||
The Avadhūta is a Kṣatriya and a great yogi, of this there is no doubt;
even a Vaiśya may become his true self, and even a Śūdra attains the same world as him.
A Brahmin obtains the full fruit and shall attain liberation;
a Kṣatriya obtains a third part of the fruit by virtue of his heroic nature.
Two parts belong to the Vaiśya, and one part belongs to the Śūdra;
O Caṇḍikā, except for the Brāhmaṇa, there is no renunciation (saṃnyāsa) for others.
If one should do so elsewhere out of delusion, that man is a refuge for sin;
O Goddess of gods, O beloved of life, one should listen with a sense of secrecy. (14.12)

O lady of beautiful countenance, O Goddess of the gods, a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) should always practice the five principles; however, if death does not occur within twelve years [of such practice], [the goal is attained]. 14-13.
And she herself, renowned as Ānanda, became Sarasvatī in her twelfth year; this is the account of the Avadhūta—listen, O Daughter of the Mountain! (14.14)
Whether in a forest, a sacred seat (bhārati), a city, or even a mountain, having settled in one place, one should practice the desired meditations and so forth. (14–15)
That mantra which is the refuge proclaimed by the wise knower of Brahman—possessing the finest hair and a mass of matted locks—he should always practice with a joyful disposition. (14–16)
O daughter of the mountain, that great hero is to be sought even within the lowest wombs—he who is learned in various scriptures and skilled in various rites. (14–17)
He who indeed meditates upon a woman with the state of being the Goddess—he alone is a hero in Bhārata, a possessor of great knowledge, and one who has conquered his senses. (14–18)
p. 23) With arms raised high, the hero with disheveled hair and naked body—he who is the best of men should meditate upon him with equanimity. (14-19)
Without one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevī), no one is proclaimed to be a true hero,
whether at the seats of various lords of gods, in sacred fields, or in places of pilgrimage.
One should constantly perform circumambulation and should worship with diligence;
likewise, one should always practice meditation on the deity as well as the worship of the venerable Guru.
O Goddess, he whose devotion is perfectly steadfast possesses the inner sacrifice, neither womb nor seed, and is both a hero and a city-dweller; he belongs to the stage of the Avadhūta.
Kālī will be pleased with him; what on this earth cannot be accomplished? Having beheld the Avadhūta, one should perform worship as if to Śambhu himself. (14–23)
One should diligently offer the five principles (pañcatattva) according to one's capacity;
without the five principles, bliss does not arise at all.
Therefore, indeed, there is no worship for you through the state of devotion.
Thus, O beloved, have I described to you the characteristics of the Avadhūta. (14.25)
By means of this mere consciousness, a person attains the state of Śiva;
it must never be given to one who is deceitful or devoid of devotion. (14.26)
This tantra must be kept strictly secret at all times, even unto death, from one who is devoid of devotion to the guru and from one who is intent on reviling the ultimate reality.
One should not cause it to be heard by one who lacks devotion, for the loss of accomplishment arises;
[it may be taught] only occasionally to one’s own son or to a high-souled disciple.

O Daughter of the Mountain, if there should be fitness for it, one should cause it to be heard by one endowed with devotion; having heard it, [one should protect it] with great effort, as if it were one's own womb.
This has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Stage of the Avadhūta," in the glorious Nirvāṇatantra, within the dialogue between Caṇḍikā and Śaṅkara. || 14 ||
It is completed; may there be auspiciousness.
